name: Tear trough filler
lead: Tear trough filler is the injection of a dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid (HA), into the tear trough, the groove or hollow that runs from the inner corner of the eye diagonally down across the lower eyelid and upper cheek. Practitioners use it to soften the shadowed hollow and the tired appearance associated with infraorbital hollows, and some describe it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.[1][2][3]

The tear trough is regarded as a technically demanding area. A 2022 systematic review of HA technique found no standardized evidence-based approach to injecting filler there, whether with a hypodermic needle or a microcannula, and a separate systematic review of delayed complications reported that side effects are generally mild and transient but that delayed complications can occur.[2][3]

Published evidence includes case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and registered trials of HA products for infra-orbital hollows.[1][2][3][6][7] In looksmaxxing forums, under-eye filler is discussed as a subtle correction with little visible change to the rest of the face, with users sharing cost and recovery impressions.[10]
infobox: Lower eyelid surgery, platelet-rich plasma, jawline filler

paras: The tear trough, or nasojugal groove, is the depression below the lower eyelid. Filler placed along it adds volume to reduce the hollow and shadow. A 2011 ophthalmic plastic surgery case series framed HA filler for the tear trough as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.[1]

A review of the HA literature notes that, despite well-documented risks, injection in this area is not standardised, and compares needle and microcannula use.[3] A surgeon-reported series of 1,452 tear trough applications describes a three-point tangent technique.[6]

A consecutive interventional case series reported one surgeon's 18-month experience with HA gel (Perlane) as a tear trough filler: 198 eyes of 100 patients, mostly female (87 percent) and white (89 percent), with a mean follow-up of 5.1 months and an assessment that included masked grading of photographs and a satisfaction survey.[1]

Systematic reviews have examined delayed complications after tear trough filler and the HA techniques used.[2][3] Registered trials include a randomized comparison of an HA filler (RHA Redensity Eye) versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows, tear trough deformity and wrinkles (NCT04577898, 248 participants, completed), a pilot phase 4 study combining two HA fillers for lower-eyelid rejuvenation (NCT00852241, 18 participants), an 11-participant prospective evaluation of infraorbital filler (NCT05694286), and a 73-participant satisfaction study of periorbital Juvéderm fillers with botulinum toxin (NCT05647551).[7][8][9][15]

Alternative biological approaches are also registered, including platelet-rich fibrin for tear trough rejuvenation (NCT03313934, 10 participants, status unknown) and a platelet-rich plasma study for the nasojugal fold that was withdrawn before enrolling participants (NCT03255681).[11][12]

A systematic review of delayed complications after tear trough filler reported that side effects are generally mild and transient but that delayed complications may occur, and set out to catalogue them from the published literature.[2] A case report described orbital compartment syndrome after tear trough filler injection.[4]

Wikipedia lists common filler effects such as bruising, redness, pain and itching, rarer infection and allergic reactions, and rare but usually permanent blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries.[13]

Google Trends analyses have examined public interest in cosmetic facial procedures during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and fluctuations in searches for cosmetic procedures.[5][14] These analyses address general interest rather than tear trough filler outcomes.

On looksmax.org, one user posted about having tear trough and jaw filler, describing it as giving small corrections that are immediately noticeable in person without looking artificial, with only some swelling and little downtime, and reporting a total cost of about 450 US dollars from a plastic surgeon with strong reviews. The poster added that the difference was hard to capture in photographs.[10]

timeline.event: Case series of HA filler for tear trough rejuvenation as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery published.[1]
Systematic reviews of delayed complications and of HA injection techniques for the tear trough published.[2][3]
Series of 1,452 tear trough applications describing the three-point tangent technique published.[6]
Case report of orbital compartment syndrome after tear trough filler published.[4]

lore.intro: Tear trough filler is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-downtime way to correct under-eye hollows alongside other facial fillers.[10]

claims.claim: Tear trough filler gives a noticeable correction without looking plastic
claims.believers: One user who had under-eye and jaw filler described the changes as small, immediately noticeable in person and natural-looking, with some swelling but almost no downtime.[10]
claims.experts: A case series of 100 patients assessed photographs and patient satisfaction after HA tear trough filler, and systematic reviews describe side effects as generally mild and transient, with delayed complications possible.[1][2]

claims.believers: The same poster reported that the treatment cost about 450 US dollars in total.[10]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified that compare costs, which vary by clinic, product and country.

card.summary: HA filler placed in the under-eye hollow as a subtle, quick alternative to eyelid surgery; delicate area with rare serious complications.
card.aka: Under-eye filler, infraorbital hollow filler, nasojugal groove filler
card.note: No standardised injection approach; delayed complications and rare orbital events reported.

quick.overview:
Tear trough filler uses hyaluronic acid injected under the eye to soften the hollow and shadow running from the inner corner of the eye across the cheek. It is promoted as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.

Published evidence includes a 100-patient case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and several registered trials of HA products for infra-orbital hollows.
quick.mechanism: The gel adds volume along the tear trough groove, reducing the depth of the hollow and the shadow it casts. Injectors use either a needle or a blunt microcannula, and a review found no standardised preferred approach.
quick.risks: Reviews describe side effects as generally mild and transient, such as swelling and bruising, while delayed complications can occur. A case report described orbital compartment syndrome. Wikipedia reports that blindness from filler embolization is rare but usually permanent. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.
